topic: Why you walk into a room and forget why
title: Why You Forget Things Walking Into a Room
voiceover: Why did you walk in here again? It's called the doorway effect, and it's real. In 2011, Gabriel Radvansky and colleagues had people carry objects through virtual rooms, then tested their memory. People forgot more after passing through a doorway than after walking the same distance inside one room. The leading explanation: your brain files experiences into 'events,' and a doorway marks a boundary, so the old thought gets filed away. Researchers still debate the details, but it happens to healthy young brains too. So go back to the room where you had the thought. The scene itself often brings the memory back. Or hold your goal in mind by repeating it before you move. Tomorrow: why something you just learned suddenly seems to follow you everywhere.

description: Walking through a doorway can make you forget why you entered the room. Researchers think doorways mark 'event boundaries' that make your brain file the old thought away. Source: Radvansky, Krawietz & Tamplin (2011), 'Walking through doorways causes forgetting', Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology.
accuracy_note: The doorway effect is documented in lab studies, but researchers still debate the exact mechanism (event boundaries vs. context change). Returning to the original room to restore context cues is supported by broader research on context-dependent memory, not just this study.
